The arrow keys and W A S D move the map while held

commit.message:
The intern can keep PNI and IX ports ahead of their traffic (closes #234)

A new standing order, Keep peering headroom, works like the transit one: it
keeps each PNI and IX port above a multiple of today's traffic (1.25x to 3x).
A single port at a POP with several routers gets a second port in a LAG; any
other port moves up to the smallest port size that fits, or the biggest the
router takes. If the preferred move cannot be done it tries the other one.

It pays through the same actions as a click (ACT.pni, ACT.lagP, ACT.buyIx,
ACT.lagIx), is off by default, has the Headroom and Budget dials and the
per-POP switch, and keeps to the cash floor. A PNI augment on order is waited
for, router ports an augment will take are not promised twice, and nothing
is bought while a DDoS flood is live, since the flood counts as port usage.

The intern's monthly bill figure (opsMoNow) now counts IX ports too.

card's filtering, and take a new one beyond that; 250 ms after the zoom stops they are

commit.message:
WebGL map: keep the pictures' keys, the waves and the clouds out of the garbage

to paint each even when the picture was already there, concatenated a prefix onto every
key, made an array per city per copy of the map for its place on screen, and rebuilt
the waves' and the clouds' arrays. Keys are now kept per city (packed into one number for
the yes/no parts), per label text and look, per stamp and scale, and joined again only
when the picture changes; pictures already painted are found before any closure is
made; the card's and the 2D map's pictures are two maps, so keys need no prefix; the
cities' places and the POP lights are computed in place; the waves and the clouds are

commit.message:
WebGL map: give the card up for 2D when it runs out of memory without saying so

A card short of memory may refuse a texture or a buffer without throwing: the call only leaves OUT_OF_MEMORY for
getError(), which nothing read. Refused, the 64 MB atlas drew every city, label and marker as a black box while the
map stayed on the card (seen in Chromium by refusing it).

The big uploads now read it (glMem()): the atlas, the land for each zoom level, the tubes once a day, the cables.
The atlas tries 2048 px (16 MB) before giving up; any other refusal is the card's error, so draw() gives WebGL up
for the session and draws the same frame again in 2D. getError() is never read on an ordinary frame: each read waits

tubes refused, leave the map in 2D in that frame with no glitch for the player; panning reads no error.

commits.subject: WebGL map: give the card up for 2D when it runs out of memory without saying so

2D map: hold its pictures to 48 MB, letting go of those unused the longest

The 2D map keeps a canvas per picture, and the list was capped only by its length (1 400). A long zoom on a big
network paints every city again at each step of its scale, so a pinch from 0.6 to 3.2 and back held 181 MB of
pictures (the TTL save: 179 MB) where one frame uses 2 to 23 MB.

At the end of a frame over 48 MB, the pictures it did not use go, those unused the longest first, down to 36 MB, and
each canvas let go is emptied (0×0) so its pixels are freed without waiting for the collector. The frame's own
pictures are never let go, so a screen that needs more keeps what it needs. Finding a picture now marks it as used.

commit.message:
WebGL map: take a lost context back, and let it go for Always 2D

The first loss of the WebGL context gave the card up for the session. A context can come back (a driver reset; on a
phone, sometimes just leaving the app), so a phone that went to another app came back to the slower 2D map until the
page was reloaded. Always 2D, chosen in Settings, kept the context and its 64 MB atlas for a map drawn in 2D.

A loss now leaves the 2D map drawing while the context is away (glLost(): the event is cancelled so the browser may
give it back), and everything on the card is built again on the same context when it comes back (glRestored(),
glForget(): glInit() runs as for the first frame). A card lost more than GL_LOSSES (2) times is given up for the
session, so a card that keeps failing does not keep the map switching. Always 2D lets the context go through
WEBGL_lose_context and Auto asks for it back, the same path, never counted as a loss; a context the browser gives back
after the player chose Always 2D is let go again. Without the extension, and for the GPU benchmark's switches
(mapGl(on,false)), the context is kept as before. The listeners and the overlay's wrappers are set once.

Diagnostic info says when the map waits for a lost context. Tests: webgl-context-restore (7), and the loss test of
webgl-out-of-memory now waits for the context instead of giving it up.

commits.subject: WebGL map: take a lost context back, and let it go for Always 2D

commit.message:
WebGL map: check the pictures sent to the card at most once a second

A frame that sent pictures read getError() to know whether the card took them. In every browser WebGL runs in another
process, and each read waits for it to finish everything sent so far, uploads included: a wait on the main thread on
exactly the frames that already cost the most (a pan or a zoom sends pictures on most frames, up to 321 in one).

The card keeps an error until it is read, so one read a second still finds a refusal: the pictures are now checked at
most every GL_MEM_EVERY (1 000) ms, and a picture refused in between shows at worst as a dark box until then, after
which the map goes to 2D as before. The first pictures sent into a new atlas are still checked at once, where a card
that allocates it lazily refuses. The cost could not be timed here (no Vulkan driver on this machine for Chromium to
reach the graphics card); the change bounds it whatever it is.

Tests: webgl-out-of-memory reads at most twice in two seconds of panning, and a refusal after the first check gives
the map to 2D within a second.

Alien waves priced against their fiber; crews halve a build at most (#203)

route sold out to its market earned 11 to 35 times its lease and the
gear paid back in one to three months. A wave now rents for 30% of the

commit.message:
Customers come and go: contracts, renewals at the market price, growth, haggles and leaving (#178)

Every customer now signs for a term (enterprise and hosting 1-3 years, wholesale and circuits 2-5,
fiber pairs 10-20). When it ends most renew at today's bandwidth price, happy ones often grow to
the next size, a few with competitors around ask for a discount 30 days ahead (match, meet halfway
or let go in Deals; no answer matches), and some leave: unhappy ones because of the service, others
acquired, bust, insourced, moved (they stay if you have a POP there), multihomed, project ended,
a cheaper bid, or now and then one of the odder reasons (never more than one every 60 days).

The bandwidth market is flat for six months, then about 10% cheaper a year, slowed by dearer
hardware, moving in a slow three-year cycle and pushed up during a shortage. New offers and
renewals are priced in it; one renewal moves a price at most 25% down or 10% up.

Nothing happens in a first term. Rolls are hashes of the customer and its term, never Math.random,
so seeded games keep their stream. Old saves get renewals spread over the next year. Happy
customers of a year or more send a referral about every six weeks. The dashboard's Customers tab
shows customers won and lost each month and why, renewals due and the market; customer rows show
the contract end.

The differential fuzz now leaves out state fields only this checkout has, so a new feature's state
does not fail the comparison with main while everything both games share must still match.

commits.subject: Customers come and go: contracts, renewals at the market price, growth, haggles and leaving (#178)

commit.message:
A sales desk: the engineer turned salesdroid, the shark, or the CEO

From customer level 2, one person runs sales at a time, next to the NOC intern:
- The engineer turned salesdroid ($9k/mo) books you into every network operators' meeting 30 days
  ahead at the usual ticket price, brings 40% more offers (half as many again while a meeting's glow
  lasts) but never the huge deals, and their customers leave less often at renewal (half as often
  for the nerdy ones: HFT, ISPs, universities, L2). Haggles badly.
- The shark ($15k/mo) brings bigger sizes at 25% more, takes a month of each deal as commission,
  oversells half of them with a requirement the network does not meet yet, never brings technical
  customers, makes selective peering desks want 25% more traffic, wins most haggles, and their
  customers leave 50% more often.
- The CEO (free) signs the biggest internet customer the network can take on the golf course every
  50-80 days at 30% off, often with a promise nobody checked, signs about a third of the offers you
  decline anyway, and has opinions. He cannot be fired: a board meeting brings a VP of Sales a month
  later.
Customers remember who signed them (by), which the renewals read. Every roll is a hash of the day
or the deal, so games without a salesperson keep their random stream.

The differential fuzz also leaves out buttons for actions main does not have yet.

commit.message:
Fabric ports at 10G, 100G or 400G, in LAGs; fabric customers only when they fit

A fabric (NNI) port comes in 10G, 100G or 400G, as fast as the router
takes and no faster than 400G, and bundles into a LAG of up to eight
members like transit, IX and PNIs. Each member takes a router port (10G
on a breakout, a quarter of one) and pays the monthly price; upgrading
moves and pays for every member. 10G and 100G keep their prices, 400G is
$3,000/mo. A model change that would strand a 400G fabric port is refused,
and saves drop fabric ports that make no sense.

The NNI requirement counted what the port already carried but not the
offer's own bandwidth, so an offer passed as long as the port was not
already over and auto-accept took customers that did not fit. It now
counts the offer too.

Closes #140, closes #307.

commit.message:
PNIs and IX ports are both peering: traffic leaves at the nearest one (#298)

Routing tried every PNI (rank 1) before any IX port (rank 2), like a
local-pref above peering, so a PNI in London pulled New York's traffic
across the Atlantic even with the same network at the New York IX. PNIs
now route at rank 2 with the IX ports, nearest first. At the same distance
the PNI goes first: an IX port counts as PNI_TIE (0.001) further away,
far below any link weight (at least 1). Distances compare as
(Da-Db)+(dta-dtb) so exits at one distance stay exactly equal, and the
POP-local shortcut skips lists that mix PNIs and IX ports. Backup only and
RouteScript's prefer pni keep their say. The traceroute, the reference
allocation in the tests and the RouteScript help follow.

commits.subject: PNIs and IX ports are both peering: traffic leaves at the nearest one (#298)

commit.message:
A day that reroutes no longer stops the page at x8: every routing it needs goes to the route worker

The day split of #312 on its own, from 3.0.0, without its routing core, save or map changes. On a big network at
x8 the game stopped whenever a day rerouted: after a failure, an event, the NOC intern's shift or the sales desk's
signing, dayPost() routed on the page.

* The day is a generator (dayRun(), dayPreRun(), dayPost()): each yield is a compute() it needs. dayTick() answers
  them on the spot (tests, fallback); in play rwGo() posts each one to the route worker. A failure (failureRun()), a
  DDoS and Auto-RTBH (ddosNewsRun()), the chaos monkey's snip (mkSnipRun()), an event's cut (eventRun()), the
  intern's shift (opsRun()) and the sales desk (slAutoRun(), its trials answered by the worker with offerTrial())
  are steps of the day. fireFailure(), opsDay() and slAutoDay() still play them in one go.
* yield DAY_REST lets a long day draw a frame between two steps (half a frame, 3 to 8 ms, RW.budget). One day in
  flight at a time, resting or routing: the clock waits for the day, and a half day is never saved.
* UI.tick is set around every step (dayStep()), so quiet notifications hold in play, not only in dayTick().
* The daily mood check works out the land islands once per pass over the customers (TERR), instead of walking
  every land link for each customer afraid of sharks. This fix is thesysadmindev's, from #310; here the islands are
  worked out again if something routed meanwhile (RW.gen), since the mood loop can now rest between customers.

Same game either way: tests/day-steps.test.js plays a second page as the worker and compares each day with
dayTick(), the intern on every order, failures, events, DDoS and the monkey forced.

Thanks to thesysadmindev for the profiling in #310 that pointed at the reroutes, and for the sharks fix.

commits.subject: A day that reroutes no longer stops the page at x8: every routing it needs goes to the route worker

commit.message:
The intern upgrades optical transport

A new standing order, Upgrade optical transport. On fiber that is full
and runs above a level, it moves the line system up one size (the
Upgrade click), or trades the smallest lit channels for the biggest
optic that fits, one at a time (setChCount; the old optics go to
spares). With a line system chosen, every fiber below it is moved up,
both steps in one night if need be, cold or not.

A line system swap is a day without the fiber, so only where another
live path joins its cities, no customer rides it, and routing the
network without it serves as much as today (one compute, measured
against today's routing). One fiber is tested and swapped a night,
and a fiber that failed is left alone for a week (not saved), so the
order costs at most one routing more, and only on a night with a
fiber to try.

commit.message:
The page stays free while big networks play: ambient map at 30 fps, saves in the worker, less to carry back

The game plays exactly as before; only what holds the page changes.

* mapStill() tells three cases apart: still (drawn once a second), ambient (only the animation clock moved: drawn at
  most every 29 ms, so 30 fps on 60 and 120 Hz screens) and moving (camera, pointer, selection, network: every frame).
  The animations follow the clock, so they keep their speed.
* save() skips the storage write when the text is the one the slot already holds (SLOT.txt) and no write is on its
  way; leaving the page still writes. A big autosave that moved on is packed, turned into text, stamped and
  compressed in the route worker (rwSave(), rwGzip()); the page only writes what comes back. A lost worker hands its
  pending saves back to the page (rwSaveBack(), rwGzBack()).
* Less crosses back from the worker: R.efg stays there while R is its own last answer (RW.wR, efg 0), R.egDesc comes
  as 0 or as the entries that changed (rwDescOut()/rwDescIn()), what crossed each link travels as typed arrays decoded
  on demand (rwLOut()/rwLIn()), and the full ports (hotMap) come along with R. Every message is read in order
  (rwMsg()), so both sides always hold the same last answer.
* Idle frames build the diverse-paths map and the latency floors a millisecond at a time (diversityWarm(),
  latWarm()), before the first offer asks.
* Diagnostic info shows how fast days really come: speed asked, speed held, how long a day takes (15-day-pace.js).
* perf-bench: "The NOC intern's shift: opsDay()" and, in Chromium, "One game day in play: page time only", a day
  played with the real route worker counting only the time it holds the page.

Tests: frame-pacing, day-pace, save-size, persist, route-worker (efg as typed arrays, hotMap from the worker),
day-steps (a second page plays the worker: answers without R.egDesc, with only its changes, posts without R.efg,
renewal haggles answered through the worker), intern-dark-fiber-worker, webgl-zoom-sprites, speed.

commits.subject: The page stays free while big networks play: ambient map at 30 fps, saves in the worker, less to carry back

commit.message:
Routing core made once, list orders kept, and Auto-TE's detour searches cut: same routing, much less work

The game plays exactly as before.

* The core of compute() (rankPass, directPass, sendGroup, send, push, carry, altPath) is ROUTE in 29-route-core.js,
  built once by routeCore(): made inside compute() they were new functions every call and V8 threw away their code.
  Exits are read by number from typed columns (USED, CAPX, CIX, HPX, VISX), each list is an object of one shape.
* The route cache keeps, for each list and source city, the order routing tries it (xOrder()); a list whose exits,
  cities and preferences are unchanged on the same graph keeps its orders when other exits change (rcExitKeep()).
* Auto-TE: pairs with no detour are marked (TEF), exits that cannot help are skipped (dud()), one failed search
  answers the next ones, dijkstraTo() searches in arrays kept between calls, teSearch() runs on the graph as flat
  arrays and picks up where the last search from the same POP stopped.
* The PNI/IX tie-break (#298) reaches the core.

Tests: route-cache, routing-reference, speed (the fast core against the plain path, Auto-TE on crowded meshes with
POPs outside the core, picked-up searches counted).

commits.subject: Routing core made once, list orders kept, and Auto-TE's detour searches cut: same routing, much less work

commit.message:
The intern and customers' promises counted once per network: ports, caches and PNIs in one pass, shared searches

The game plays exactly as before.

* The NOC intern plans every POP in one pass: portsAt() counts router ports for all cities at once (routers, ports
  and cache orders; the ports job keeps ports in use and reserved by city between two jobs), cachePlan() sorts the
  boxes by POP once and cityShSum() sums a city's shares once per table, pniFlows() reads every POP's flows from
  routing's columns (R.flc) in one pass and pniWant() gives the weekly PNI round its sort key from typed columns.
  pniBatchRun() lets a frame through every few networks; pniQuote() looks existing PNIs and ports up from the batch.
* A dark fiber's capacity asks optG() once per run of identical optics (dfLit()); linkDown() and ownGlass() ask
  dfOn(), whether it carries anything for you, without the sum unless an optic is out or managed waves are sold on
  it. terrIslands() tests !l.sub first.
* Latency: latGraph() lists each city's links once in S.links order (typed arrays), latRun() is the same search with
  the same sums, latPairs() searches once per city for a boutique's finance routes and the latency offers.
* Diverse paths: divGraph()/divOn() number the cities and risks once; promiseCheck() shares a diversity graph, the
  land islands and one latency search per origin across every customer when the intern weighs taking a fiber out,
  and spots0() shares the graph for sovereign offers.

Tests: day-steps (cache planner, ports at every POP and flows from columns equal the old ways; the PNI round through
pniBatchRun), fiber-lit-and-latency (with failed optics and managed waves), shared-promise-checks, intern-personas.

Moving waves checks the room the broker would sell: bandwidth for managed waves, and what is kept back

Managed waves need a channel as big as the wave and their bandwidth spare after your own traffic and
the share kept back, on leased fiber too. A move bumps CM_V so their capacity follows them, merging
needs the same size, and alien waves leave the kept-back channels alone. Pinned customers' badges
share one path graph per routing result.

commits.subject: Moving waves checks the room the broker would sell: bandwidth for managed waves, and what is kept back

commit.message:
Kept exit orders also check each exit's kind

An exit that turned from an exchange into a PNI at the same place in the list, city and
preference kept the order made for the exchange, which sorts behind a PNI at the same
distance, so the cached routing could differ from routing without the cache (#320 review).
The exit signature now includes the kind. Also drops the unused e.vis.

commits.subject: Kept exit orders also check each exit's kind

commit.message:
Clear the open code scanning alerts

- auto-release.yml: the by-hand test run passes github.sha (what it got anyway) instead of an
  output that also reads workflow_run.head_sha, so CI never checks out a ref a workflow_run
  handed over in a job that uses caches (cache poisoning, 7 alerts in ci.yml).
- tests/harness.js: the script splitter also matches end tags like </SCRIPT > (bad HTML
  filtering regexp).
- Tests paste the fixture saves into the page with lit(), which escapes what could end a
  script or a string, instead of plain JSON.stringify (improper code sanitization).

commits.subject: Clear the open code scanning alerts
